lesson.body:
Are tasting notes just fancy words? Researchers in the Netherlands gave a computer about 76,000 wine reviews by 13 **critics**, people paid to judge wine. From the words alone, it could tell red from white and rosé, and name the grape most of the time. The critics shared plain words, like cherry, plum and vanilla.

A **tasting note** is a few lines that record what a wine is like, so you can remember it and compare it later. You need only four parts, in the same order every time:
• Style: what kind of wine it is.
• Structure: how it feels in your mouth.
• Flavours: two or three things you smell and taste.
• Verdict: what you think of it.
You still smell before you sip.

Style comes from your eyes. Tilt the glass over white paper and write the colour and how deep it looks: pale, medium or deep. Tasters borrow simple colour words: lemon for a yellow white, ruby for a bright red. Add bubbles if there are any.

**Structure** is the parts you feel rather than smell: sweetness, **acidity** (the sourness that makes your mouth water), **tannin** (the drying feel strong black tea leaves in your mouth), alcohol and **body** (how heavy the wine feels). Give each a level: low, medium or high. For sweetness, say dry (not sweet), off-dry (a touch sweet) or sweet; for body, light, medium or full.

Alcohol has no fruit smell, but you feel it as **warmth** in your mouth and the back of your throat, most after you swallow. More alcohol, more warmth. The % vol on the label tells you how much: most **still wines** (wines without bubbles) sit between about 11 and 14.5%. Too much alcohol for the wine burns, and tasters call that wine **hot**.

For flavours, pick two or three, no more. Start broad, with fruit, flowers, spice or oak (vanilla and toast from the barrel), then narrow down: fruit, citrus, lemon. 'Lemon and green apple' says far more than 'nice' or 'elegant'.

The **verdict** has two halves. Is it well made? Look for balance, where no single part sticks out, and a finish, the flavour that stays after you swallow, that lasts. Then: do you like it, and would you buy it again? A wine can be well made and still not be for you.

A whole note fits on one line. A crisp white, one with plenty of acidity: 'Pale lemon white. Dry, high acidity, light body. Lemon and green apple. Balanced, long finish, would buy again.' A big red: 'Deep ruby red. Dry, high tannin and alcohol, full body. Blackcurrant and vanilla. Balanced, but too big for me.'
lesson.summary: Turn what you see, smell and feel into one short note in four parts: style, structure, two or three flavours and a verdict, with alcohol's warmth included.
lesson.title: Put it into words: a simple tasting note

bank.key: A tasting note records what a wine is like so you can remember it and compare it later.
opts: Proving you are a wine expert
Impressing the people at your table
bank.q: What is a tasting note for?
bank.remember: Notes are for remembering, not showing off.
bank.why: A short note turns one glass into something you can learn from next time.

bank.key: Style, structure, flavours, verdict: the same four parts, always in the same order.
bank.q: A useful tasting note follows the same four parts in the same order every time.
bank.remember: Same parts, same order, every glass.
bank.why: A fixed order lets you compare two notes line by line and stops you forgetting a part.

bank.key: In the style part, 'pale lemon' is a colour word: a light yellow white wine.
opts: The grape it was made from
bank.q: In the style part, what does 'pale lemon' describe?
bank.remember: Style lemon is a colour, not a flavour.
bank.why: Tasters borrow simple colour words, so 'lemon' here is about what you see, not what you smell.

bank.key: Acidity and body are structure: things you feel. Blackcurrant is a flavour, deep ruby a colour.
bank.q: Which two belong in the structure part of a note?
bank.why: Structure tells a reader how the wine is built, whatever it smells of.

bank.key: Body, how heavy a wine feels, is rated light, medium or full.
bank.q: For body, the simple levels are light, medium and full.
bank.why: Simple words that everyone shares make notes easy to read and compare.

bank.key: Alcohol has no fruit smell. You feel it as warmth in your mouth and throat.
bank.q: You notice alcohol mostly as a fruity smell in the glass.
bank.remember: Alcohol is felt, not smelled as fruit.
bank.why: Knowing where to look helps you spot a high-alcohol or hot wine.

bank.key: Alcohol shows as warmth in your mouth and the back of your throat, most after you swallow.
opts: Mouth and throat, after you swallow
On the very tip of your tongue, at first
In your nose, before you take a sip
On your gums, as a drying feel
bank.q: Where do you feel a wine's alcohol most?
bank.remember: Warm throat: alcohol. Dry gums: tannin.
bank.why: The drying feel on your gums is tannin, so the two are easy to tell apart.

bank.key: Real things you could buy or sniff, like cherry and vanilla, say far more than praise.
bank.q: Which flavour line is most useful in a note?
bank.why: Months later, 'cherry and vanilla' still tells you what the wine was like; 'nice' does not.

bank.key: Two or three flavours are enough. Start broad, then narrow down if you can.
bank.q: A good note lists as many flavours as you can find.
bank.remember: Two or three flavours, no more.
bank.why: A short, sure list is easier to trust and to remember than a long, guessed one.

bank.key: A balanced wine has no single part, such as acidity, tannin or alcohol, sticking out.
opts: The flavour stays a long time
The wine is dry, not sweet
bank.q: In a verdict, what does balance mean?
bank.why: Balance is one of the clearest signs that a wine is well made.

bank.key: Quality and liking are separate halves of the verdict, and they can differ.
bank.q: A wine can be well made and still not be to your taste.
bank.remember: Good wine, wrong wine for you: both true.
bank.why: Noting both shows you which styles you enjoy, not just which wines are good.

bank.key: 'Dry, high acidity, light body' is structure: sweetness, acidity and body, each given a level.
bank.q: In the crisp white's note, which line is the structure?
bank.remember: Structure lines are full of levels.
bank.why: Spotting each part in a finished note helps you write your own the same way.

A whole note fits on one line. A crisp white, one with plenty of acidity: 'Pale lemon white. Dry, high acidity, light body. Lemon and green apple. Balanced, long finish, would buy again.' A big red: 'Deep ruby red. Dry, high tannin and alcohol, full body. Blackcurrant and vanilla. Balanced, but too big for me.'
deep_notes: The team, from Radboud University in the Netherlands and Ghent University in Belgium, tested an old claim: that smells cannot really be put into words, so wine reviews are gibberish. Naming the grape was the hard part, with around 30 to choose from. The most useful clues were not grape names but words for smells, tastes and colours, such as cherry, ripe and red. In a separate study, beginners used more liking words, such as 'pleasant', while experts named more things, such as vanilla.

Wine schools use a longer form. The Wine & Spirit Education Trust, a large British wine school, teaches four headings: appearance, nose, palate (the mouth) and conclusions. The Court of Master Sommeliers, which trains restaurant wine experts, uses a similar grid. Your four parts squeeze those forms into one line each. The schools write the nose before the mouth; your note puts what you feel before what you smell. Either way, a fixed order stops one sense rushing ahead of the others.

The colour words come from the professionals' forms. Whites run from lemon-green to lemon, gold, amber and brown; reds from purple to ruby, garnet, tawny and brown. Depth is just pale, medium or deep: look down through the middle of the glass and see how much of the white paper shows through. Clarity counts too. A cloudy wine can be a sign of a fault, so it is worth a word in the note.

Pros use finer steps. Their forms add medium-minus and medium-plus between the levels, so acidity can be 'medium-plus'. For a beginner, three levels are plenty and far easier to agree on. The trick is to compare. If a wine makes your mouth water more than most, call the acidity high. If your gums feel as dry as after strong black tea, the tannin is high. Your levels sharpen with every wine you taste.

Alcohol does more than warm. It makes a wine feel a little fuller and can make a dry wine seem faintly sweet. High alcohol is not a flaw by itself: a big, ripe red with plenty of fruit and tannin can carry 14.5% with ease, and the warmth feels pleasant. It only becomes hot when the rest of the wine is too light to balance it, and the burn hides the fruit.

Order your flavours from strongest to faintest, so the first word is the one anyone would notice. Add a clue to where a flavour comes from if you can: fresh fruit hints at a young wine, dried fruit or leather at an older one, and vanilla or toast at an oak barrel. Two or three words keep you honest. Past that, most beginners start guessing, and the note gets harder to trust.

The finish is the easiest quality clue to measure: just count the seconds after you swallow. Professionals judge quality by balance, finish, how intense the flavours are and how many layers they have. Liking is separate. One taster loves high acidity; another finds it too sharp. Even experts disagree about balance, because people's mouths differ. That is why your verdict keeps two halves: one for the wine, one for you.

deeper.body: Wine school forms often add two in-between steps, medium-minus and medium-plus, so acidity, tannin, body and finish each get five levels. On the best-known form, alcohol keeps just three: low, medium and high. Sweetness has its own words, from dry through off-dry, medium-dry, medium-sweet and sweet to luscious, very sweet indeed. Finer steps help experts compare notes. For your own notes, three levels are plenty.
deeper.title: Pros rate in five steps, not three

deeper.key: Alcohol is rated low, medium or high, while acidity, tannin, body and finish get five steps.
deeper.q: On the best-known professional form, how many levels does alcohol get?
deeper.why: Your three-level note already matches how professionals rate alcohol.

deeper.body: The alcohol figure on a label is allowed some leeway. In the EU and the UK it may differ from the real figure by up to 0.5 percentage points, or 0.8 for some wines, such as sparkling wines. In the United States, a wine of 14% or less may be up to 1.5 points off, within limits. So treat the label as a guide, and let your mouth give a second opinion.
deeper.title: The label number can be a little off

deeper.key: Labels may be slightly off: up to 0.5 points for most EU wines, 1.5 for many US wines.
deeper.q: A wine label always shows the exact alcohol figure, to the decimal point.
deeper.remember: The label is a guide, not a lab test.
deeper.why: Two wines labelled 13% can differ a little, so your sense of warmth still matters.

deeper.body: Professional forms end with a question beginners rarely ask: drink now, or keep? A young wine that may improve usually has plenty of acidity or firm tannin, concentrated fruit, and all of it in balance. Without enough fruit, keeping only lets the wine fade. Most wine is made to be enjoyed within a few years of release, so 'drink now' is the right answer far more often than not.
deeper.title: Ready now, or worth keeping?

deeper.key: Wines that age well usually have acidity or firm tannin, concentrated fruit, and balance.
opts: Light and soft, with very low acidity
Fruity, low tannin, gone in a flash
Hot, with thin and faint fruit
deeper.q: Which young wine is the best bet for keeping a few years?
deeper.remember: Structure plus fruit plus balance: worth keeping.
deeper.why: Acidity and tannin protect the wine, and enough fruit gives it something to grow into.
